rv.q: It’s a lovely Chicago play, brought thrillingly back to Broadway life.
A quietly transfixing performance from Ayo Edebiri provides reason enough to see the Broadway revival of "Proof."
Add to that Edebiri, who, while not giving the career-defining performance Parker did, is nonetheless worth seeing.
A play that I remember as being about thought now strikes me as dangerously lacking in that quality; a character I remember as complicated is, in fact, just a palatable gloss on actual dysfunction.
Despite that strong support, though, it ultimately falls on Edebiri to hold the play’s center of gravity.
They all have moments, but the equilibrium is off, and the pace lags when Claire is offstage.
Proof may yet add up to something, but it's going to need a little more genius.
It all adds up to one exceptional piece of theater.
Proof, 25 years later, pulls us in and grips us in a manner that might surprise even the author.
An altogether first-class production that speaks to the brain and the heart in equal measure, a winner in every way.
Broadway just got smarter and deeper thanks to the return of David Auburn’s Proof, a complex, curvy, and thoroughly compelling play motored by a math-related mystery.

Cheadle makes an impressive Broadway debut. Playing that other daughter, Kara Young manages to show yet another facet to an awesome talent that has already brought her two Tonys, as well as much acclaim off Broadway. Her repertoire of both wacky and down-to-earth ingénue characters runs the gamut.
The cast assembled here is easily one of the best on Broadway right now.
Proof remains the same appealing play that it was a quarter century ago, when it ran for more than two years and won three Tony Awards and the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
More a competent production than a revelatory one.
But Kail’s spiritless revival fails to tap into the play’s specific collision of expansive ideas and fervid emotion.
Auburn’s drama remains a sturdily constructed mystery that deepens as it progresses.
